title: Youth Activism and Change: Birmingham to Today
teacher_intent: Highlight how youth-led civic action can shift public policy and public opinion.

student_needs.language: Offer bilingual glossaries for key civic vocabulary.
student_needs.processing: Embed movement breaks between source rotations.

compelling_question: How do young people force change when adults resist it?
supporting_questions: What conditions in Birmingham pushed youth to join the Children's Crusade?
How did different stakeholders react to the student marches?
Which evidence shows that youth activism shifted national responses?
Where do we see similar civic strategies in today's climate justice movements?

sources.title: "Letter from Birmingham Jail" (excerpt)
sources.origin: Martin Luther King Jr., April 1963, open letter to local clergy
sources.value: Explains strategic nonviolent direct action and moral justification for youth marches.
sources.citation: King, Martin Luther Jr. (1963). Letter from Birmingham Jail.

sources.title: Photograph set: Children's Crusade and firehoses
sources.origin: Bill Hudson, Associated Press, May 1963, Birmingham, Alabama
sources.value: Documents state response to youth activists and sways national public opinion.

sources.title: "Youth Lead the Climate Strike" (news analysis)
sources.value: Provides contemporary comparison showing youth strategies and policy impact.
sources.citation: Doe, J. (2019). Youth Lead the Climate Strike. National News.

extend_move: Plan a brief testimony for a local school board meeting proposing a student-led civic action that draws lessons from Birmingham.

exemplars.title: 1968 Chicago Student Walkouts
exemplars.description: Students demanded better school conditions and curriculum relevance during the civil rights era.

exemplars.title: Ayotzinapa Student Protests
exemplars.description: Families and students organized to demand government accountability after the 2014 disappearances.

interest_prompts: What problems in your community make you want to speak up?
Which movements or leaders inspire you to take action?
How do you prefer to share your ideas—art, speeches, social media, meetings?
iteration_focus: Support each learner in independently applying causation analysis when designing civic action pathways.

dok_overrides.Level 1: List two cause-and-effect links from the Children's Crusade that show why youth were central to the movement.
dok_overrides.Level 3: Analyze two sources that disagree about the impact of youth arrests in Birmingham. Decide whose reasoning is stronger and justify with evidence.

interest_responses.prompt: Choose a type of situation where causation, civic participation might appear. Pick a number or describe your idea (connect it to the concept).
interest_responses.response: Environmental or climate challenge that needs collective response

interest_responses.prompt: Who should hear what you discover? Choose an audience or add your own.
interest_responses.response: Local civic leaders (school board, city council, youth commission)

interest_responses.prompt: How would you most like to share your findings?
interest_responses.response: Visual or multimedia story (poster, video, digital exhibit)
